text: Buy a warm roll from Ilka's basket.
response: Ilka hands it over in a twist of paper and says the crust is better when the oven's in a good mood.

text: Ask Ilka where she does her baking.
response: Ilka bakes in a neighbour's oven before light, her flour sack nearly empty, eyes on every shop window.

text: Buy her flour before she asks.
response: Ilka turns the sack over twice, like she's checking it's real, and goes back to the oven humming.

text: Tell her the corner shop could be hers.
response: Ilka laughs, then stops laughing, and looks across the street at it for a long while.

text: Put her name to the empty storefront.
response: Ilka puts her hand flat on the door, the way you'd touch a sleeping animal.

text: Walk her through the rebuilt shop.
response: Ilka walks the new floor end to end, counting where the ovens will go under her breath.

text: Put your own name to the storefront.
response: Ilka wipes her hands on her apron and keeps wiping them long after they're clean.

text: Take the rebuilt shop for yourself.
response: Ilka had already measured the window for her bread. She doesn't say so.

text: Sell her flour at the price she'll pay.
response: Ilka counts out the coins slowly. The loaves will be smaller this week.

text: Tell her there's nothing here for her.
response: Ilka doesn't argue. She just starts looking at the road out of town.

text: Buy a twist of tea from Aldo's counter.
response: Aldo weighs it on the brass scales as carefully as gold and rings the door bell for you as you go.

text: Stay a while as Aldo tidies the shelves.
response: Aldo keeps a little book of what he owes under the till, and a letter from his daughter by the sea on top.

text: Put three against what he owes.
response: Aldo crosses a line out in his little book and doesn't thank you, which is how you know.

text: Ask about his daughter, and listen.
response: Aldo talks about his daughter's kitchen by the sea until the kettle goes cold.

text: Say the coast would suit him.
response: Aldo looks at the shelves like he's already saying goodbye to them.

text: Help him pack the shop up.
response: Aldo wraps the scales in a shirt so they won't knock on the cart. He leaves the bell on the door.

text: Mention to his creditor that he's behind.
response: The creditor writes something down. Across the street, Aldo is still sweeping his step.

text: Buy his stock at what he'll take.
response: Aldo helps you carry it out. He holds the door, because he always holds the door.

text: He is sitting on the step. He doesn't look up.
Ask the man in the rubble what used to stand here.
response: Ves says he built the houses on this street with his own hands, and looks at them like they owe him nothing.

text: Sit on a fallen beam beside Ves.
response: Ves says his tools sit in the pawnshop window, and nobody's asked him to build a thing since the roof came in.

text: Buy his tools back out of pawn.
response: Ves weighs the hammer in his hand and his whole arm remembers.

text: Stand in the ruin and tell him it can be rebuilt.
response: Ves kicks a fallen beam, then crouches and looks at where it used to sit.

text: Find him the first small job.
response: Ves is up a ladder before you've finished talking. He's whistling something old.

text: Hire his hands out and keep the difference.
response: Ves takes what you hand him and doesn't ask what the job paid.

text: Tell him the ruin is coming down.
response: Ves leaves the tools where they are. He doesn't come back for them.

text: Stop and ask Mara about the well.
response: Mara says the well is older than the town, and she's kept it since she was a girl with a ribbon in her hair.

text: Help Mara haul up a bucket.
response: Near the top the rope gives a little and Mara grips it hard. It's been fraying all season, she says.

text: Splice the fraying rope for her.
response: Mara runs the splice through her fingers, and the bucket comes up without a jerk for the first time in weeks.

text: Draw the day's water before she wakes.
response: Mara finds the trough full and stands over it with her shawl still on, smiling at the water.

text: Sell her a length of rope at your price.
response: Mara pays, and knots the old rope back on anyway, to make the new one last.

text: Tell her the rope will hold another winter.
response: Mara lowers the bucket the way she always has. The rope creaks, and she trusts it.

text: Nod to the watchman lighting his lantern.
response: Otto touches his cap and says the ruins are quiet at night, but someone has to stay awake for them.

text: Ask Otto how long his nights are.
response: Otto says the round is lonely and the cold corner bites. Some nights he leans on the wall and his eyes close.

text: Walk his round with him.
response: Otto talks the whole round, about nothing, like he's been saving it up for years.

text: Take the cold end of his round again.
response: Otto hands you the lantern at the cold corner without asking, and blows on his fingers.

text: Doze in his lantern-light and let him walk.
response: Otto turns his lantern down a little so it won't wake you, and walks on alone.

text: Report that he sleeps on the wall.
response: They take his lantern by morning. The wall is darker than you thought it would be.

text: Look at the dresses in the seamstress's window.
response: Lise waves you in and pins a sleeve on you without asking, talking round a mouthful of pins.

text: Bring Lise a torn hem to mend.
response: Lise squints at the needle a long while before the thread goes in. Her eyes aren't what they were, she says.

text: Thread her needles for the week.
response: Lise holds a needle up to the window and laughs, because she can see the eye again.

text: Sit and thread for her again.
response: Lise sews faster with you there. She hums the same three notes over and over.

text: Buy her last good coat cheap.
response: Lise folds the coat with care, the way she'd fold it for anyone, and says it suits you.

text: Tell her customers her stitching has gone.
response: Lise sits in the window with a dress half done, and nobody comes to collect it.

text: Ask what came in on the fishmonger's slab.
response: Per names each fish like an old neighbour and slaps the biggest, proud, though the slab is thin today.

text: Walk down to the jetty with Per.
response: Per shows you the boat his father left him and the dark seam where the sea gets in. He bails it every dawn.

text: Help him tar the leak in his boat.
response: Per runs his hand along the seam and nods to the boat, not to you.

text: Bail with him before the tide.
response: Per bails with his back to the sea and talks about his father, who also bailed.

text: Take his morning catch on credit you won't pay.
response: Per writes your name on the board by the stall. The chalk will still be there next week.

text: Cut his mooring line loose in the night.
response: In the morning Per stands on the jetty with the cut end of the line in his hand.

text: Say good morning to the widow on her step.
response: Greta says good morning back as if she'd been waiting, and tells you her husband planted the rose by the gate.

text: Stop by Greta's on a cold afternoon.
response: Greta's woodpile is low against the wall. Her husband used to split it, she says, and the axe is heavy now.

text: Split a week of firewood for her.
response: Greta brings you tea in her husband's cup and doesn't explain why that one.

text: Stack another cord against her wall.
response: Greta counts the cords by the wall and does the sum for winter. It comes out right.

text: Take her husband's tools; she won't use them.
response: Greta watches you carry the tools out. She'd kept them oiled.

text: Tell her the house is wanted by someone else.
response: Greta starts wrapping her plates in newspaper, one at a time, very carefully.

text: Ask the boy by the ruin what he's up to.
response: Hansi is skimming stones on a puddle and says, very seriously, that he's the fastest runner on the street.

text: Find Hansi out by the ditches.
response: Hansi is calling a name into the ditches. His dog ran off in the storm, he says, but it always comes back.

text: Walk the ditches with him calling for his dog.
response: Hansi calls until his voice cracks, then lets you call for a while.

text: Call for the dog again, further out.
response: Out past the last ditch, Hansi stops and listens hard, and you both hear something.

text: Sell him a story about where the dog went.
response: Hansi pays you everything in his pocket and runs off the wrong way, sure of it.

text: Tell him the dog is dead. It isn't.
response: Hansi stops calling. Somewhere out past the ditches, the dog is still waiting.

text: Look in at the schoolroom window.
response: Tobias is teaching letters to a roomful of children, spots you, and makes them all say good morning.

text: Wait for Tobias after lessons.
response: Tobias writes with a chalk stub so small it pinches, and frets over the slow ones falling behind at the back.

text: Give him the chalk you were saving.
response: Tobias writes the date on the board in big letters, just because he can.

text: Sit with the slow ones while he teaches.
response: Tobias catches your eye over the slow ones' heads and mouths, thank you.

text: Sell the school's last books for what they'll fetch.
response: Tobias reads the next lesson to them from memory. The shelf behind him is bare.

text: Tell the parents he drinks.
response: Fewer children come on the second morning. Tobias sets out the same number of slates.

text: Ask the woman with the bag where she's off to.
response: Anneke says a baby's coming out at the far farms, and she caught most of the children in this town herself.

text: Meet Anneke on her way home at dusk.
response: Anneke walks the far road home in the dark with no lantern. The oil costs too much, she says, and she's tired.

text: Walk her home from the far farms.
response: Anneke tells you about every baby she's lost the road for, and the one that came early in a ditch.

text: Take the lantern and walk her out again.
response: Anneke falls asleep walking, nearly, with her hand on your sleeve.

text: Charge her for the lantern oil.
response: Anneke pays for the oil out of the eggs a farmer gave her. She doesn't argue.

text: Let her walk the dark road alone.
response: Anneke goes out without the lantern. She knows the road. She says she knows the road.

text: Watch the cooper hoop a barrel.
response: Klaus drives the hoop down with a mallet and grins at you, sweat on his nose, as the staves pull tight.

text: Ask Klaus who buys his barrels.
response: Klaus nods at the stacks in his yard. Nobody, lately. The brewer's cutting back, and the barrels just sit.

text: Take two barrels off his hands.
response: Klaus taps the barrels as you roll them off, listening, proud of the sound.

text: Buy another barrel you don't need.
response: Klaus knows you don't need it. He picks you a good one anyway.

text: Haggle him down below his cost.
response: Klaus takes it. He'll go without hoops this week to make it come out.

text: Tell the brewer his barrels leak.
response: The brewer's cart goes past Klaus's yard without stopping.

text: Hand the laundress your shirts.
response: Sofie sniffs your shirts and says she's seen worse, which is about the kindest thing she says to anyone.

text: Collect your shirts from Sofie.
response: Sofie hands them over with her knuckles cracked red from the lye, and the mangle squealing behind her.

text: Bring her the good salve for her hands.
response: Sofie rubs the salve in and keeps her hands open on her lap, as if they were new.

text: Turn the mangle for her an hour.
response: Sofie sits down on an upturned tub for the first time all day and just breathes.

text: Pay her late, and less.
response: Sofie counts it twice to be sure, and then says it's fine, and folds your shirts.

text: Say the linen came back grey.
response: Sofie washes the same sheet three times. It came out white the first time.

text: Look in at the cold forge.
response: Emil is sweeping it out though nothing burns, and says it was his father's forge, and is his now, he supposes.

text: Ask Emil about his father.
response: Emil says his father left him the forge and a pile of ledgers he can't follow, full of debts to strangers.

text: Sit with him over his father's ledgers.
response: Emil finds his father's handwriting in the margins and goes quiet over it.

text: Take a share of the debt onto your name.
response: Emil looks at your name next to his father's and doesn't know where to put his hands.

text: Buy the forge tools at a widow's price.
response: Emil helps you lift the anvil onto the cart. He knew it would go one day. Not today.

text: Tell the creditors where the tools are kept.
response: They come at first light. Emil stands in the empty forge with the fire still in.

text: Stop at the hives by the ruin.
response: Rike lifts a frame with bare hands and tells you the bees know her by smell, and don't mind you much yet.

text: Ask Rike how the honey's coming.
response: Rike says the hives sit in the ruin's shadow now, the bees are going quiet, and she's down to the last jars.

text: Help her move the failing hives to the sun.
response: Rike leans close to the hive in the sun and listens. The hum is louder.

text: Carry the frames out for her again.
response: Rike lets the bees walk over her bare wrist and doesn't brush them off.

text: Take a jar of the last honey for nothing.
response: Rike watches you take it and says nothing. There aren't many jars left on the shelf.

text: Leave the hive lids off overnight.
response: In the morning Rike walks the row of hives, lifting each lid, and stops speaking.

text: Ask the ferryman the fare across.
response: Jonas names a fare and then waves it off, because you look like you've walked a long way already.

text: Wait at the landing with Jonas.
response: Jonas says the river's dropped so low the boat drags on the bar, and he hauls it over by himself.

text: Help him drag the boat over the low bar.
response: Jonas pushes off into the deep water and lets out a long breath like he's been holding it since spring.

text: Pull the rope with him again at dusk.
response: Jonas sings on the far side of the rope, badly, and doesn't care that you hear.

text: Cross without paying; he won't ask twice.
response: Jonas ties up behind you without a word, and rows back across for nobody.

text: Tell travellers the ferry has stopped running.
response: Jonas waits at the landing all afternoon with his hand on the bell.

text: Put your head round the inn door.
response: Hedda calls from behind the bar that the soup's on and the fire's lit, and you're welcome either way.

text: Ask Hedda how trade is at the inn.
response: Hedda shows you room after room with the beds made and nobody in them. The carters stopped coming, she says.

text: Sweep out her empty rooms with her.
response: Hedda opens a window in every room, as if someone were coming.

text: Sit in her empty room so it isn't empty.
response: Hedda sets two cups on the table, and then, after a moment, a third for no one.

text: Take a bed and a meal, and settle later.
response: Hedda chalks it up behind the bar under the other names, where the chalk is thickest.

text: Tell the carters her beds have lice.
response: The carters' wagons go through without stopping. Hedda keeps the fire lit anyway.

text: Watch the cartwright shave a spoke.
response: Viktor runs his thumb along the spoke and tells you a wheel is only as good as its worst spoke.

text: Ask Viktor what he's working on.
response: Viktor shows you a wheel he promised and can't finish. The tyre needs someone to hold the rim, and he's alone.

text: Stay late and help him finish the wheel.
response: Viktor spins the finished wheel on its pin and watches it till it stops, true.

text: Hold the rim while he sets the tyre.
response: The tyre hisses on and Viktor laughs out loud, once, at the steam.

text: Take the wheel he made for someone else.
response: Viktor looks at the empty spot on the wall and starts the same wheel again from the hub.

text: Tell his customer the order will not come.
response: Viktor finishes the wheel anyway and leans it by the door for someone who isn't coming.

text: Stop at the herbalist's drying racks.
response: Nell crushes a leaf under your nose and tells you what it's for, and what it isn't, and what it might be.

text: Ask Nell why her shop is so quiet.
response: Nell says people cross the street now. There's talk about her and her remedies, and talk sticks here.

text: Stand in her doorway where people can see you.
response: Nell's first customer in a week comes in behind you, nervous, and buys mint.

text: Buy from her in front of the others.
response: Nell wraps it in paper and ties it with string, like it was something fine.

text: Take her remedy and pay her in talk.
response: Nell listens to your talk and nods, and lets you go with the jar.

text: Repeat what they say about her, louder.
response: Nell takes her bunches of drying sage down from the window and closes the shutter.

text: Watch the ropemaker walk his rope.
response: Bram walks backwards down the ropewalk, twisting, and tells you rope is just patience you can tie a boat with.

text: Ask Bram where his hemp is.
response: Bram opens the shed and the smell comes out. Rain got into his hemp, and he can't bring himself to burn it.

text: Help him spread the spoiled hemp to dry.
response: Bram sniffs the hemp, then sniffs it again, and says it might do yet.

text: Turn the hemp with him again.
response: Bram starts twisting a strand while you turn, just to feel the hemp take.

text: Buy his good rope for the price of the bad.
response: Bram coils it for you neatly. It's the best rope he has, and he knows you know.

text: Tell the boatmen his rope is rotten.
response: Bram twists rope all afternoon that no one will buy, because his hands don't know how to stop.

text: Wave to the goatherd on the high field.
response: Ilse waves back with her crook and calls each goat by name as they come down, as if introducing you.

text: Climb up to Ilse's hut.
response: Ilse yawns through every sentence. She's watched the field alone each night since lambing, and the foxes know.

text: Sit the night watch on the high field.
response: Ilse sleeps in the hut till dawn, properly, for the first time since lambing.

text: Take the cold watch again.
response: Ilse brings you a cup of milk still warm from the goat and sits with you at the end.

text: Take a kid from the herd; she's lost count.
response: Ilse counts again in the evening and gets one less, and counts again.

text: Leave the gate open behind you.
response: Ilse spends the whole day on the high field calling them in, one name at a time.

text: Ask the stonemason about the old wall.
response: Ansel tells you he laid that wall as a young man, and points out the stone he carved his initials on.

text: Watch Ansel at work on the new course.
response: Ansel bends to a stone, stops, and rubs his back. He can't lift the big ones now, he says, not like before.

text: Carry the stone he can't lift any more.
response: Ansel sets the stone you carried and pats it, the way you'd pat a horse.

text: Shoulder his load again, and say nothing.
response: Ansel says nothing either. The wall goes up a course before dark.

text: Take the job he's too slow for now.
response: Ansel watches you lay the first stone from across the road. He doesn't correct you.

text: Say his walls are coming down.
response: Ansel walks the length of his old walls with his hand on them, checking.

text: Stop at the candlemaker's window.
response: Dorte holds up a candle to show you its colour and tells you good light is a kind of company.

text: Ask Dorte why her window is dark.
response: Dorte says tallow's dear and she's scraping the pot. She sells every candle and sits in the dark herself.

text: Bring her tallow from your own store.
response: Dorte dips the first candle and holds it up to the light, pleased with the colour.

text: Bring her tallow again.
response: Dorte has started leaving a lit candle in the window for when you pass.

text: Buy her candles cheap and sell them dear.
response: Dorte wraps them in paper for you. Two streets over, you'll sell them by the pair.

text: Tell her buyers her candles smoke.
response: Dorte trims the wicks shorter and shorter, trying to find what's wrong with them.

text: Step aside for the drover's cattle.
response: Rurik tips his hat as the cattle push by and says they're good beasts, all of them, even the stubborn ones.

text: Ask Rurik which way he's taking them.
response: Rurik says the river road washed out and he doesn't know a way round. The beasts are getting thin waiting.

text: Help him find a way round the washed-out road.
response: Rurik whistles the beasts through the gap and laughs when the last one makes it.

text: Walk the long way with him again.
response: Rurik walks with his hand on the lead cow's neck and tells you her name.

text: Take his beasts' grazing for your own.
response: Rurik's beasts stand at the fence looking at the grass. He moves them on.

text: Send him down the road that's gone.
response: Rurik is gone two days. He comes back with one beast fewer and doesn't say where.

text: Watch the potter at her wheel.
response: Maike pulls a bowl up out of the clay without looking down, and laughs when you lean in to see how.

text: Ask Maike when she'll fire the pots.
response: Maike shows you the crack through her kiln. The last firing broke inside it, she says, nearly every pot.

text: Help her re-lay the cracked kiln.
response: Maike lights the kiln and sits right up against its warmth, like an old friend.

text: Pack the kiln with her again.
response: Maike packs the last pot in and holds her breath, then lets it go.

text: Take the pots that survived, for nothing.
response: Maike looks at the empty shelf where the good ones stood, and wedges more clay.

text: Tell her the clay here was always bad.
response: Maike stops at the wheel with her hands wet and looks at the clay for a long time.

text: Lift your cap to the sexton at the tower.
response: Stefan nods from the tower steps and says he knows everyone in town by the sound of their feet on the path.

text: Ask Stefan why the bell is silent.
response: Stefan says the bell rope snapped and he's too old for the climb. The town has been guessing the hour since.

text: Climb up and re-hang the bell rope.
response: The bell sounds across the whole town, and Stefan stands under it with his cap off.

text: Ring the hours for him.
response: Stefan sits on the step with his eyes shut and counts the hours with you.

text: Take the lead off the roof; no one looks up.
response: It rains in the night. Stefan puts a bucket under the drip and doesn't look up either.

text: Let the bell stay silent and say nothing.
response: The town forgets what hour it is. Stefan climbs the tower, and climbs back down.

text: Admire the cloth on the weaver's loom.
response: Ebba lets you touch the cloth and tells you the pattern came from her grandmother, who got it from hers.

text: Watch Ebba weave a while.
response: Ebba's shuttle keeps snagging. The loom's warped in the damp, she says, and every row comes out crooked.

text: Help her true the warped loom.
response: Ebba throws the shuttle and it runs straight across for the first time all winter.

text: Wind her bobbins for the evening.
response: Ebba weaves into the dark, and the pattern comes out like she meant it.

text: Take the cloth she wove for another.
response: Ebba starts the cloth again from the first thread. She doesn't sing at the loom this time.

text: Tell the market her cloth runs short.
response: Ebba measures every bolt twice, then three times. They were always full length.

text: Stop at the mill for a word.
response: Lukas comes out white to the elbows and shakes your hand, and now you're floury too, and he laughs about it.

text: Ask Lukas why the mill sounds wrong.
response: Lukas says the millstone's worn smooth and grinds coarse. He'd dress it, but it's not work for a man alone.

text: Help him dress the millstone.
response: Lukas feels the new grooves with his thumb and grins with flour in his eyebrows.

text: Turn the stone with him again.
response: The stone turns sweet and Lukas listens to it the way other men listen to music.

text: Take your flour and settle at harvest, maybe.
response: Lukas writes it down on the mill door, under the other harvests that never came.

text: Say his flour has grit in it.
response: Lukas sifts his own flour three times looking for the grit, and doesn't find any.

text: Taste a sliver of the cheesemaker's cheese.
response: Gunda watches your face as you chew, nods, satisfied, and tells you how long that wheel has been ageing.

text: Ask Gunda to show you her cellar.
response: Gunda opens the cellar door on water up to the bottom step. Her cheeses sit on planks above it, sweating.

text: Bail out her flooded cellar.
response: Gunda stands in the cellar with the water gone and laughs at her wet boots.

text: Carry the wheels up out of the wet.
response: Gunda rubs salt into the rinds by the warm wall, telling each wheel it's safe now.

text: Take the cheese that's still good.
response: Gunda lets you take it. The ones left behind are going soft.

text: Tell them her cellar is fouled.
response: Gunda opens her cellar door to show people. No one comes down to look.

text: Watch the thatcher up on a roof.
response: Arne calls down from the ridge that he's thatched every roof you can see, and some you can't any more.

text: Ask Arne how the reeds are this year.
response: Arne says the reed beds need cutting before the frost, the days are short, and there's only him to cut them.

text: Cut reeds with him while there's light.
response: Arne cuts as the sun goes, quick and quiet, so you won't stop before he does.

text: Bundle the reeds with him again.
response: Arne ties the last bundle and sits on it, and offers you half his bread.

text: Have him thatch yours first, and pay last.
response: Arne thatches your roof first. His own still drips at the corner.

text: Tell the village his roofs let water.
response: Arne climbs up on his own roof in the rain to show it doesn't leak. Nobody watches.

text: Ask the apothecary's girl for a remedy.
response: Pia fetches the jar the apothecary points to and dusts it off, quick and bright, with a smile for you.

text: Ask Pia what the jar says.
response: Pia goes red. She knows the jars by colour and shape, she says. The words on the labels won't keep still.

text: Read the labels aloud until she knows them.
response: Pia says the word back to you, slowly, and then again, faster, proud of it.

text: Sit and read the hard ones again.
response: Pia reads one all on her own and looks up to see if you heard.

text: Let her guess, and buy what she mislabels.
response: Pia hands it over with a careful smile. She'll get it right one day. Not on yours.

text: Tell the apothecary she can't read.
response: Pia sweeps the floor of the apothecary's shop and isn't allowed near the shelves now.

text: Call over to the tanner by his pits.
response: Henrik comes to the fence instead of making you come in, and apologises for the smell before he says hello.

text: Ask Henrik why trade is so slow.
response: Henrik says the wind carries the pits into town and people complain, so they don't buy. They want them gone.

text: Help him move the pits downwind.
response: Henrik stands upwind of his own pits for once and breathes all the way in.

text: Dig with him again at the new pits.
response: Henrik leans on his spade and tells you the town will come back round. Maybe.

text: Buy his leather at the price the smell allows.
response: Henrik takes it, and holds his breath, and you can't tell if it's the smell.

text: Complain about the smell where it carries.
response: Henrik scrubs his hands until they're raw, and they still smell of the pits.

text: Look at the coloured glass in Birgit's window.
response: Birgit tilts a pane so the colour falls on your hands and says that's the only reason she does any of it.

text: Ask Birgit about the boarded window.
response: Birgit says her whole shipment of glass came off the cart in pieces. She's been picking through it ever since.

text: Help her sort the glass that survived.
response: Birgit holds a whole pane up to the sky and the light comes through it clean.

text: Sweep the broken glass with her again.
response: Birgit picks a small piece of blue out of the sweepings and puts it in her pocket.

text: Take the whole panes for your own window.
response: Birgit wraps the panes in straw for your cart. Her own window still has a board in it.

text: Say she broke the shipment herself.
response: Birgit stops leaving her glass out in the sun to show the colours.

text: Nod to the man black with soot.
response: Matthias wipes his hand to shake yours, which doesn't help, and says he burns charcoal, as if it didn't show.

text: Ask Matthias where he gets his wood.
response: Matthias says the forest's been shut to him by order and his clamp is nearly out. He doesn't know who to ask.

text: Speak for him about the closed forest.
response: Matthias stands at the back while you speak, black to the elbows, and nods once.

text: Speak for him again, to someone who matters.
response: Matthias doesn't say anything on the walk home. He just keeps looking at the trees.

text: Buy his last charcoal for nothing.
response: Matthias shovels it into your sack and the last smoke goes out behind him.

text: Agree that the forest should stay shut.
response: Matthias's clamp goes cold. He sits beside it at night as if it were still burning.

text: Watch the spinner at her wheel.
response: Runa spins without looking and tells you she could do it in her sleep, and some nights she has.

text: Ask Runa why her basket's empty.
response: Runa says the sheep were sold over the hill and there's no wool to be had. Her wheel turns on nothing now.

text: Bring her wool from your own back.
response: Runa pulls the wool between her fingers and starts spinning before you've gone.

text: Bring her what wool you can spare.
response: Runa spins your wool into something soft and gives you back a little of it.

text: Take her yarn and pay her in thanks.
response: Runa says you're welcome and means it. Her wheel stops early that night.

text: Tell them her yarn breaks.
response: Runa tests every hank against her own strength. None of them break.

text: Stop at the farrier's post.
response: Erik pats a passing horse that isn't his to pat and tells you he can read a horse's mood by its feet.

text: Ask Erik why his post is empty.
response: Erik says everyone takes their horses to the town smith now, closer and quicker. He keeps his fire hot anyway.

text: Bring your horse to him, not the town smith.
response: Erik holds your horse's hoof in his lap like it was something precious.

text: Bring the neighbour's horse to him too.
response: Erik has two horses tied at his post today. He doesn't say anything, but he's whistling.

text: Take a shoeing and forget to pay.
response: Erik waves you off. Later he writes it on the wall, with a little horse drawn next to it.

text: Say his nails lame the horses.
response: Erik shoes the same horse again, slower, checking every nail.

text: Pick up a basket at Thea's stall.
response: Thea tells you she wove that basket on the riverbank in the rain, and it has never dropped an egg yet.

text: Ask Thea where she gets her willow.
response: Thea says the willow by the river wants cutting and stripping before it hardens, and her mother used to help.

text: Cut willow with her by the river.
response: Thea weaves the first basket right there on the bank, quick, and gives it you.

text: Strip the willow with her again.
response: Thea's hands are green to the wrist and she's telling you about her mother.

text: Take a basket each time you pass.
response: Thea leaves one by the door each morning now, in case. She doesn't say why.

text: Cut the willow stand back to nothing.
response: Thea stands in the stubble where the willow was and doesn't know where to put her knife.

text: Hail the woodcutter coming in from the trees.
response: Jost drops a load of logs with a grunt and tells you there's no smell like fresh-split oak, none at all.

text: Ask Jost why his woodpile is short.
response: Jost shows you his axe. The head wobbles on the haft, and he's scared it'll fly off mid-swing and take an ear.

text: Help him re-hang the loose axe head.
response: Jost swings the axe and it rings true, and he takes a whole tree down for the joy of it.

text: Swing with him until the cord is cut.
response: Jost stacks the last of the cord and leans on it, red-faced and pleased.

text: Take his cut wood; he'll blame the road.
response: Jost curses the road and the carters on it. He goes back out in the cold for more.

text: Leave the head loose and say it's fine.
response: Jost swings, and the head comes off and flies, and he looks at his empty hands.

text: Say hello to the dairymaid with her pail.
response: Alva tells you each cow's name and temper, and offers you a sip from the pail as if it were wine.

text: Ask Alva how the milking went.
response: Alva shows you the pail, near empty. Her best cow's gone dry, and the farmer counts every drop she brings in.

text: Sit up with the dry cow through the night.
response: Alva sleeps against the cow's warm side, and you let her.

text: Sit up with her again.
response: By morning there's a little milk again. Alva laughs at the pail like it told her a joke.

text: Take the last of the milk for yourself.
response: Alva scrapes the bottom of the pail for the farmer and hopes he won't look.

text: Tell the farmer she let the cow go dry.
response: The farmer shouts. Alva stands in the yard with the empty pail and doesn't answer.

text: Look at the clocks in Nikolas's window.
response: Nikolas comes out to tell you which clock is right, and which are lying, and which he keeps for company.

text: Ask Nikolas what he's mending.
response: Nikolas shows you an open clock, and his hands won't hold still over it. The fine work is slipping from him.

text: Hold the glass steady while he works.
response: Nikolas closes the case and the clock ticks, and he listens like it's his own heart.

text: Hold the light for him again.
response: Nikolas works until the light goes, and then a little after, because you're still holding it.

text: Buy the clock his hands can't finish.
response: Nikolas wraps the clock without its hands. It will never say a time.

text: Say his clocks all run slow.
response: Nikolas sets every clock in the shop against the church bell, and they're right.

text: Stop by the netmaker on the quay.
response: Sanne's hands never stop while she talks, and she tells you she can mend a net in the dark by feel alone.

text: Ask Sanne about the heap of torn net.
response: Sanne says a storm tore the long net and she's mending it by herself, a hand's width at a time, all winter.

text: Sit and mend net with her.
response: Sanne shows you a knot her grandmother taught her, and then makes you do it.

text: Mend the long net with her again.
response: Sanne's hands and yours go along the long net together till you meet in the middle.

text: Take a net and settle after the season.
response: Sanne writes your name on her slate. It's a short slate, and she rubs out a lot.

text: Tell the boats her nets part.
response: Sanne pulls every knot of a net tight that wasn't loose, to be sure.

text: Salute the old soldier by the door.
response: Wilhelm returns it smartly without getting up, names his regiment, and tells you kindly that you did it wrong.

text: Ask Wilhelm how he gets by.
response: Wilhelm says the town owes him a pension and has forgotten. He wrote in his bad hand, and nobody answered.

text: Write to the town about his pension.
response: Wilhelm reads it over your shoulder and sits up straighter in his chair.

text: Write again, and this time sign it.
response: Wilhelm salutes you, a little wrong, and laughs at himself for it.

text: Drink what's left of his pension with him.
response: Wilhelm tells the same war story three times, and you let him, and the jug is empty.

text: Tell them he was never in the regiment.
response: Wilhelm takes his medal off his coat and puts it in a drawer.

text: Knock on the door across the landing.
response: Wren opens a crack, then wider. They've lived across the landing for ages and never learned your name.

text: Meet Wren on the stairs with the coal.
response: Wren is hauling a coal scuttle up alone, step by step, and says supper's just bread again, eaten standing up.

text: Carry their coal up the stairs with yours.
response: Wren holds the door with their foot and says you needn't have. They leave it open a while after.

text: Eat supper with them instead of alone.
response: Wren pulls the second chair out from under the coats. It hasn't been sat in for a long time.

text: Ask them to stay.
response: Wren carries their one box across the landing, and that is all it takes.

text: Let them cover the rent this week.
response: Wren counts it out on the table and doesn't ask when you'll pay it back.

text: Tell them you were always better alone.
response: Wren takes the box back across the landing. The door clicks, and then the stairs.

text: Read with them by the window.
response: Pim follows the line with a finger and gets the long word on the second try.

text: Buy them a proper meal.
response: Pim eats with both hands and talks with their mouth full, and you let them.

text: Walk them round the market and say their name to people.
response: Pim holds your sleeve past the fish stalls, then lets go of it by the well.

text: Send them to carry sacks for the miller.
response: Pim comes home white with flour and puts the coins on the table without a word.

text: Tell them to stay out from under your feet.
response: Pim goes very quiet and finds somewhere small to sit.

text: Put the storefront in their name.
response: Pim stands under the sign and reads their own name on it, slowly, twice.

text: Put the rebuilt shop in their name.
response: Pim runs a hand along the new wall, where the builder's marks still show.
